messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The night Kwame’s life fractured began with a routine walk home from his first week at a downtown tax consulting firm. The air was cool, but the narrow service corridor behind the building funneled sound and shadow. A man stepped from the doorway, his voice rising into a sharp shout that froze Kwame in place. Before he could bolt, the heavy metal door clicked shut behind him, sealing him in the confined space. The rape was brutal and prolonged, marked by the attacker’s ragged breathing, the taste of copper and cheap whiskey coating Kwame’s tongue, and the relentless visual of the man’s face inches from his own. When the man finally stumbled away, leaving Kwame trembling on the concrete, the silence that followed was heavier than the violence. He fled, but the corridor, the shout, and the closing door were already etched into his nervous system as a blueprint for survival, explaining exactly why those specific sounds and spaces would forever feel inescapable. On his third week, walking past a construction site, a foreman’s amplified shout echoed off the pavement. The sound acted as an immediate catalyst, transforming ordinary urban noise into indicators of imminent harm. Kwame’s breath hitched and his muscles coiled, instantly convinced he was facing the same suffocating danger as that night. These auditory shocks reliably fed directly into his sense of threat. He stopped going to the campus library or the coffee shops he used to frequent, because walking into unfamiliar buildings meant he couldn’t map the exits or predict where a threat might materialize. Even strangers approaching him on the sidewalk to ask for directions sent a jolt of panic through his chest; he was certain they were looking for an opening, just like the man in the corridor. The environment had become a minefield, and his body reacted to every potential spark as if the fire were already burning. These sensory intrusions inevitably pulled him back to the event. When a male colleague at the firm raised his voice to make a point during a tax review, the sound acted like a key turning in a lock, unlocking a flood of frozen photographs from that night: the flickering fluorescent light, the scuffed boots, the way the door latch had caught. More unsettlingly, the smell of stale coffee in the breakroom or the taste of a colleague’s mint would suddenly flood his mouth with the exact metallic tang of blood and whiskey from the assault. He would stare at his screen, unable to process the quarterly reports, his throat tightening as the past overwrote the present without warning. The cues were not just reminders; they were the doorways through which the memories forced their way back into his daily life. As the weeks stretched into months, the memories themselves began to dictate his daily navigation. The images and tastes were so visceral that they left him hyper-alert to every male voice and every heavy door in his building, making him scan for threats before he even recognized them. The past was constantly pulling his attention outward, ensuring that the sight of a man, the sound of a door, or the memory of a taste would always circle back to the same dread. He had come to believe that the only way to survive was to anticipate the exact moment a trigger would appear, so he began cataloging every male presence and every metallic click of a latch. The memories were no longer passive intrusions; they were active sentinels, constantly directing his gaze toward the very things he feared most. He had initially thought that avoiding unknown territory would keep him safe, but this pervasive sense of impending danger inevitably pulled the event back into his mind. The fear wasn't just in his head; it was a physical current that ran backward, reactivating the very cues he tried to ignore. Sometimes the emotion hit him without any image at all, a pure wave of terror that left him gasping in the breakroom. When he felt that sudden spike of alarm, his hands would tremble, and he would instinctively flinch or pull away if anyone brushed his shoulder. The dread was the spark, and the memories were the fuel, each one feeding the other in a tightening loop. His attempt to outrun the threat only ensured that he remained permanently tethered to the event. This rigid avoidance reshaped his work and relationships. At the firm, he refused to take the service elevator, opting for the long stairwell to avoid being trapped alone with other men. He requested client meetings only in the main conference room with the door propped open, and he began leaving his desk the second he heard raised voices from the accounting department. When a senior partner tried to pat his shoulder during a team debrief, Kwame recoiled so sharply he knocked over his water bottle, his heart hammering against his ribs as if he were back in that corridor. The more he restricted his movements to manage the threat, the more the triggers multiplied, turning a manageable job into an exhausting exercise in risk assessment. Now, at eighteen, Kwame has stopped trying to manage it alone. What finally drove him to a clinician’s office was the night he couldn’t leave his apartment for three days after hearing a shout in the hallway, realizing his work was suffering and his social life had completely vanished. He is exhausted by the constant calculation of safety, terrified that he will never stop flinching at a familiar sound or that the memories will keep dictating his life. He wants to walk through a crowded street without checking exits, to sit in a meeting without scanning for threats, and to finally taste food without bracing for a taste of blood. He is hoping, more than anything, that he can learn to trust that the past is no longer present.
